title: Stage resonance correlation notes
body:
Summary:
This is a working note from a week-long end-to-end latency audit focused on stage-level covariance (what I’m calling "stage resonance") across cohorts. The goal was to explain recent p95/p99 regressions seen in mid-to-long sequence workloads and to identify reproducible trace fingerprints we can use for alerts and targeted mitigations.

High-level findings (short):
- A consistent resonant pattern: a majority of p95/p99 outliers had an elevated batch_wait stage coinciding with a KV-cache miss spike — when both occur the tail multiplies, not sums.
- Seqlen bucket 64-512 shows the worst instability: p95s jump ~3–5x during 10–20 minute microbursts.
- Async-batcher prototype reduced observed p95 by ~35% on the 64-512 cohort during controlled replay.

Dataset and method:
- Time window: 2026-02-20 to 2026-02-26 (7d production traces + replay).
- Source: sampled end-to-end traces (1:500 sampling) from production logging + deterministic replay harness (trace replay v2).
- Cohorts: seqlen <64, 64–512, >512; kv-cache hit vs miss; single-tenant vs multi-tenant noisy endpoints.
- Metrics collected per trace: total latency, per-stage durations (tokenize, route, batch_wait, kv_lookup, model_compute, kv_write(optional), serialize, egress), token count, batch size, model-variant resolved.
- Quantiles computed: p50, p95, p99 per-cohort and per-stage.

Representative end-to-end quantiles (aggregated):
- seqlen <64: p50=22ms, p95=82ms, p99=210ms
- seqlen 64-512: p50=48ms, p95=320ms, p99=1050ms
- seqlen >512: p50=95ms, p95=820ms, p99=2200ms

Per-stage p95 breakdown (64-512 cohort, median of trace-level stage durations):
- tokenization: 6ms
- routing/dispatch: 10ms
- batch_wait: 120ms (varies widely; 90th percentile ~320ms during bursts)
- kv_lookup: 40ms (hit) / +300ms on miss (includes remote KMS/HSM for some private deployments)
- model_compute (forward + kv apply): 80ms
- serialize/egress: 18ms
- total: ~320ms (matches p95)

Fingerprinting the tail:
- Trace phenotype A (common p95): batch_wait elevated (~100–150ms) + kv_lookup mostly hits. Signature: small-to-medium batch size (2–8) formed slowly due to concurrent routing jitter.
- Trace phenotype B (p99 jumps): batch_wait high + kv_lookup miss on first tokens causing an extra model forward/regen. Signature: seqlen>256, cache miss rate spike, model_compute doubled in those traces.
- Trace phenotype C (sporadic extreme p99): external egress backpressure (upstream client slow reads) causing egress serialization to accumulate and back-propagate batch formation delays.

Key hypotheses and evidence:
1) Hypothesis: batching jitter (router scheduling variability) is the dominant amplifier of tail when combined with occasional KV misses.
   Evidence: controlled replay where we artificially increased router jitter from 2ms -> 25ms produced p95 increases matching production bursts; removing KV misses in replay removed the amplified p99 cases.
2) Hypothesis: KV misses are multiplicative because a miss triggers a cold-forward path that replays tokens (effectively double model_compute for that request).
   Evidence: traced traces where kv_lookup state=miss show two model_compute segments; aggregate model_compute in miss traces ~2x.
3) Hypothesis: serialization/egress stalls sometimes mask as compute tail but are downstream; fixing routing/batching reduces incidence by ~15% but some class remains.
   Evidence: correlation matrix shows positive covariance between serialize duration and batch_wait (r=0.42) during microbursts.

Experiments run (summary):
- Async-batcher experiment (replay): enabled async-batcher path in serving runtime for 48h replay window. Result: 64–512 cohort p95 reduced from 320ms -> 209ms (~34.7% reduction); p99 reduced 1050ms -> 740ms (~29.5%).
- KV cache prewarm patch: prewarm on cold-start reduced kv miss tail frequency by 60% in dedicated nodes but had no effect on multi-tenant noisy endpoints (root cause elsewhere).
- Edge egress yield control: small tweak to socket write batching reduced mean serialize by 10% but had marginal tail improvement.

Actionable mitigations (ordered):
1) Short-term (within 2 weeks): enable async-batcher for the 64–512 traffic routed to dedicated pools (canary to 5% then 25%). Owner: Ravi K. Impact: immediate p95 improvement in replay.
2) Mid-term (1 month): implement kv-cache prefetch heuristic keyed by recent-sequence affinity (warm predictions for continuing sessions). Owner: Priya N. Dependencies: KMS rate-limits gating.
3) Mid-term: add a stage-level alert that fires when both (batch_wait.p95 > 150ms) and (kv_miss_rate > 3%) in a 5min window. Owner: Liam O.
4) Long-term (quarter): explore a model-variant "fast-path" that tolerates stale kv responses (stale-kv fallbacks) for serving latency-sensitive endpoints. Owner: eng-serving-runtime arch team.

Tracing examples (sample ids):
- T-2026-02-21-1542: phenotype A; batch_wait 132ms; kv_hit; total 380ms; notes: small batch formed slowly due to routing spin.
- T-2026-02-23-0918: phenotype B; kv_miss triggered extra forward; model_compute segments 2x; total 1420ms.
- T-2026-02-25-0333: phenotype C; egress backpressure observed; socket write stalls.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why is kv miss spike correlated with routing jitter only in multi-tenant pools? Possible tenant interference causing resource contention (NIC/IO). Need cross-correlation with node-level metrics (NIC queue depth, CPU steal).
- How much of the observed batch_wait variance is scheduler-driven vs application-level jitter? Need microbench with blocked scheduler to isolate.

Immediate next steps (this week):
- Canary async-batcher on a dedicated pool and compare production p95/p99 for the cohort (Ravi).
- Instrument node NIC and IO queues for a 72h window to correlate with kv_miss spikes (Liam).
- Draft rollout README for the async-batcher flag and risk decider for Private deployments (Maya).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is a snapshot; many traces are archived in the trace store under project=serving-runtime/investigations/stage-resonance.
- Replay harness + dataset and scripts are on PR #842 (linked above).
- If you reproduce locally, use the "replay-v2 --cohort 64-512 --replay-mode deterministic" command from the PR.

Appendix (quick numbers table):
- baseline-64-512: p50=48ms, p95=320ms, p99=1050ms
- async-batcher-replay-64-512: p50=46ms, p95=209ms, p99=740ms
- kv-miss-traces (sample): average additional latency on miss = +300ms to +1200ms depending on KMS path.

Owners and checkpoints:
- Ravi Kapoor (canary async-batcher) — checkpoint 2026-03-12 (canary results due).
- Liam O'Connor (node-level instrumentation) — data snapshot 2026-03-08.
- Priya Nair (kv prefetch design doc) — draft 2026-03-15.

End of note.
